Scatter
skat'ter
v. (to disperse, to drive apart; rendering Hebrew puts and zarah, Greek diaspeiro and skorpizo)
A variant of shatter, from Middle English. Hebrew zarah is properly to winnow — to throw grain into the wind so the chaff blows away — which gives the scattering of a people its agricultural and judicial overtone at once.

Biblical Definition

To scatter in Scripture is God's act before it is anyone else's, and it serves three purposes. It is judgment: at Babel “the LORD did there confound the language of all the earth: and from thence did the LORD scatter them abroad upon the face of all the earth” (Genesis 11:9) — a scattering that broke a united rebellion and, in breaking it, filled the earth as the original command had required. It is the mark of a people without a shepherd: Ezekiel indicts Israel's shepherds because the sheep “were scattered, because there is no shepherd: and they became meat to all the beasts of the field” (Ezekiel 34:5) — and that chapter ends with God promising to be the shepherd himself. It is prophesied of the disciples and fulfilled in a garden: “smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered: and I will turn mine hand upon the little ones” (Zechariah 13:7). Our Lord quotes it on the night he was betrayed, so that the scattering of his own men was foretold and did not surprise him. And it becomes the engine of the mission: after Stephen's death the church “were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judaea and Samaria” (Acts 8:1), and the next verses report that they went everywhere preaching the word. James writes to the result: “the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad” (James 1:1).

Webster 1828 Definition

To disperse. God scatters at Babel in judgment, mourns a flock scattered for want of a shepherd, foretells his own disciples' scattering — and turns a persecution's scattering into the spread of the gospel.

expand to see more

SCATTER, v.t. To disperse; to dissipate; to separate or remove things to a distance from each other.

2. To throw loosely about; to sprinkle; as, to scatter seed.

3. To spread or set thinly; as, to scatter trees over a field.

4. SCATTER, v.i. To be dispersed or dissipated.

5. In Scripture, to disperse a people; I will scatter them among the heathen, Lev. 26.

Key Scripture

Ezekiel 34:5 — "And they were scattered, because there is no shepherd: and they became meat to all the beasts of the field, when they were scattered."

Zechariah 13:7 — "Awake, O sword, against my shepherd, and against the man that is my fellow, saith the LORD of hosts: smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered: and I will turn mine hand upon the little ones."

Acts 8:1 — "And Saul was consenting unto his death. And at that time there was a great persecution against the church which was at Jerusalem; and they were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judaea and Samaria, except the apostles."

James 1:1 — "James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad, greeting."

Modern Corruption

Scattering is read only as loss, so that dispersion, exile, and the breaking up of what was gathered are treated as pure defeat — when Acts 8 shows God using a persecution's scattering to sow the word.

expand to see more

Every scattering in Scripture is painful and none is merely negative. Babel broke a project and thereby fulfilled the creation mandate to replenish the earth. The exile emptied a land and produced synagogues, a preserved text, and a people who never returned to idols. The persecution after Stephen emptied Jerusalem of its church and planted the gospel in Samaria and, before long, in Antioch, where disciples were first called Christians. Luke does not moralise about this; he simply reports that they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word (Acts 8:4). A congregation losing members to distance, or a work broken up, may be watching the same providence and should be slow to name it defeat.

The principle to recover is that the sheep scatter when the shepherd is struck, and that God says so beforehand. Zechariah 13:7 is a hard verse — the sword is summoned against the man that is God's fellow, which is a claim about the Messiah's deity — and Christ applies it to himself hours before it happened. The disciples' failure that night was foretold, atoned for, and repaired; he told them in the same breath that after he was risen he would go before them into Galilee. Ezekiel 34 gives the same comfort in the same order: the flock scattered for want of a shepherd, and then I will both search my sheep, and seek them out.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew puts is to scatter or dash in pieces; zarah is to winnow, to fan away. Greek diaspeiro gives diaspora; skorpizo is to disperse a flock.

expand to see more

Hebrew puts (H6327) — to scatter, to dash in pieces; the verb at Babel.

Hebrew zarah (H2219) — to winnow, to fan, to scatter; the threshing-floor image behind exile.

Hebrew pazar (H6340) — to scatter abroad, to disperse; also to scatter gifts liberally.

Greek diaspeiro (G1289) — to sow throughout, to scatter; the root of diaspora, Acts 8:1.

Greek skorpizo (G4650) — to disperse; the wolf scattereth the sheep, John 10:12.

Usage

"Of judgment that fulfilled a mandate: did the LORD scatter them abroad upon the face of all the earth (Genesis 11:9)."

"Of a flock without a shepherd: they were scattered, because there is no shepherd (Ezekiel 34:5)."

"Of persecution turned to mission: they were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judaea and Samaria (Acts 8:1)."
